title: PKI and Mutual TLS: Certificates as Identity
intro: Ordinary TLS proves the server to the client. Mutual TLS (mTLS) also proves the client to the server, with a certificate instead of a password or token. It's how service meshes authenticate every call and how many internal APIs are locked down. You have a private certificate authority (ca.crt and ca.key) and need a client certificate for the service checkout to call https://payments.internal.

steps.prompt: Generate a 2048-bit RSA private key for the client, in client.key.
steps.explanation: A private key, which never leaves this machine.
steps.why: The private key is the identity; the certificate only vouches for it. Generate it where it will be used, so it never travels. Restrict the file (chmod 600) straight away. EC keys ('openssl ecparam -genkey -name prime256v1') are smaller and faster and are the usual choice for new systems.

steps.prompt: Create a certificate signing request from that key, with the subject common name checkout, in client.csr.
steps.explanation: A request containing the public key and the name you're asking the authority to certify.
steps.why: The CSR carries the public key and the requested identity, signed by the private key to prove you hold it. The private key isn't in it, so a CSR is safe to send to the authority. This split is the whole design of PKI: the authority certifies keys it never sees.

steps.prompt: Sign the request with the CA to produce client.crt, valid for 30 days.
expected_commands: openssl x509 -req -in client.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial -days 30 -out client.crt
openssl x509 -req -in client.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial -out client.crt -days 30
openssl x509 -req -days 30 -in client.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial -out client.crt
steps.fake_output:
Certificate request self-signature ok
subject=CN = checkout
steps.hint: openssl x509 -req -in client.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial -days 30 -out client.crt
steps.explanation: The CA signed a certificate saying this key belongs to checkout, for 30 days.
steps.why: Short lifetimes are the modern answer to revocation, which works badly in practice: a 30-day (or 24-hour) certificate that's stolen simply runs out. That only works if issuing is automated, which is what cert-manager, Vault's PKI engine, SPIFFE/SPIRE, and service meshes do. The CA's own private key is the crown jewel; in production it sits in an HSM or a managed service, never in a file on a laptop.

steps.prompt: Check the new certificate chains to the CA.
steps.explanation: The certificate was signed by this CA and is within its validity period.
steps.why: This is the same check the server will make. If it says 'unable to get local issuer certificate', the CA file doesn't contain the certificate's issuer: a different CA, or a missing intermediate. Run it before deploying a certificate, not after the handshake fails in production.

steps.prompt: Call https://payments.internal/health presenting the client certificate and key, and trusting the private CA.
steps.explanation: Both sides authenticated: you verified the server with the CA, and the server identified you as checkout.
steps.why: --cacert is who you trust; --cert and --key are who you are. Without the client certificate the server ends the handshake ('certificate required'), or a proxy returns 400 'No required SSL certificate was sent'. mTLS authenticates; it doesn't authorize. The server still needs a rule saying checkout may call this endpoint, which is what a mesh's authorization policies add.

steps.prompt:
A handshake fails with 'certificate is not valid for the name payments.internal'. Which part of a certificate must contain the hostname?
  a) The common name (CN) alone
  b) The Subject Alternative Name (SAN) extension
  c) The issuer field
  d) The serial number
Type the letter.
steps.fake_output:
$ openssl x509 -in server.crt -noout -ext subjectAltName
X509v3 Subject Alternative Name:
    DNS:payments.internal, DNS:payments.shop.svc.cluster.local
steps.hint: Modern clients ignore the common name for hostname checks.
steps.explanation: The SAN list. Clients no longer fall back to the common name.
steps.why: Go, browsers, and current curl all require the name in the SAN. A certificate with only CN=payments.internal fails even though it looks right. List every name clients use, including the Kubernetes service names. 'openssl x509 -noout -ext subjectAltName' shows what a certificate really covers.
